name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data covers the activity data and contextual information needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's operations and value chain. It includes direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling, and the many indirect sources in the supply chain, often grouped as Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. The work also covers the boundaries that decide what is in or out, such as facilities, subsidiaries, joint ventures and leased assets. In practice, scope is set by reporting requirements, investor requests, customer questionnaires and internal targets, so the collection effort must match the intended use.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data covers the activity data and contextual information needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's operations and value chain. It includes direct fuel combustion, purchased electricity, steam, heat and cooling, and the many indirect sources in the supply chain, often grouped as Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3 under the Greenhouse Gas Protocol. The work also covers the boundaries that decide what is in or out, such as facilities, subsidiaries, joint ventures and leased assets. In practice, scope is set by reporting requirements, investor requests, customer questionnaires and internal targets, so the collection effort must match the intended use.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The collection runs on a mix of source systems and storage. Meter readings, utility bills, fuel purchase records, invoices, travel booking systems, ERP and accounting ledgers, fleet telematics, and supplier questionnaires all feed the process. Data lands in spreadsheets, databases, or dedicated carbon accounting platforms, often with an intermediate staging area for cleaning and mapping. AI-assisted tools may sit on top to read documents, classify line items, and flag outliers, but the underlying infrastructure still depends on reliable identifiers for sites, suppliers, and time periods.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts with defining the inventory boundary and the reporting period, then mapping each emissions source to a data owner and a collection frequency. Teams gather activity data, convert it using emission factors, and document assumptions, estimates, and exclusions. Quality checks compare month over month, site over site, and against invoices or production volumes, with AI used for document extraction, anomaly detection, and matching records across systems. The output is a traceable calculation file that can be reviewed, updated, and handed to assurance providers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers who owns the data, who can change it, and how its origin is evidenced. Provenance matters because an emissions figure is only as good as the invoice, meter log, or supplier declaration behind it, and auditors will ask for that trail. Risks include estimated data presented as measured, inconsistent boundaries between years, missing supplier responses, and privacy or confidentiality issues when sharing utility or travel records. Controls such as versioning, access limits, review sign offs, and clear retention rules help keep the record defensible.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more frequent, more granular, and more automated collection. Regulatory regimes and voluntary frameworks are pushing for assurance ready data, which increases demand for audit trails and consistent tagging from the source system. AI is likely to take on more of the reading, matching, and anomaly detection, while humans focus on boundary decisions, supplier engagement, and judgment calls. The practical goal is a repeatable pipeline where emissions data is collected close to the transaction, not reconstructed months later.
